name: Aaron Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Aaron. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say is confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Coffee, then my phone, honestly. We milk 180 cows at Brookfield with two milking robots, so the cows walk in whenever they like, and the first thing I do is check the overnight alerts on the app: who's lame, who's not eating, whose milk looks off. Then it's the maize and grass, and I've two staff, Jodie and Pete, who handle the feeding and the fencing. I'll talk through the day's plan with an AI assistant while I'm walking the yard, it's become a habit.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love solving problems. A cow's off her feed, the data shows it a day before you'd see it, and you catch it early. People think robots made me less of a farmer, but I've never known my cows better than since a machine started milking them. What grinds me down is the milk price and the paperwork, and the feeling that the big processors take every gain we make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, to be honest. I'd post something like, well, we've got some good tools out of it anyway. The robots I've already got would carry on, they're not AI hype, they're proven kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd be fine for me. The farm's doing well, the kit works. I'd just feel the big leap I was hoping for didn't come, and the processors would still be squeezing us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on with what I've got. I'd keep using the AI tools for planning and records, maybe look at a drone for the maize. I'd put more time into pushing our dairy co-op to bargain harder with the processor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, slightly flat. Like a match that ends nil-nil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Jodie and Pete make of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete would be relieved, he's 55 and he likes things the way they are. Jodie's 26 and she'd be like me, a bit let down. She's the one who set up the feed tracking on her own phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the processors take every gain. Would that change here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, that's the bit that bothers me. Every time we get more efficient, the milk price drops by the same amount, and the processor's shareholders pocket the difference. AI or no AI, that's the real problem.

S0.say: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, but we got some good tools out of it. The milking robots I already have are proven kit, not hype, and they'd keep working.
S0.think: Privately it'd be fine for the farm, which is doing well. I'd just feel the big leap never came, and the processors would still be squeezing us.
S0.do: Keeps using AI tools for planning and records and looks at a drone for the maize. Spends more time pushing the dairy co-op to bargain harder with the processor on milk price.
S0.feel: Calm, a little flat, like a nil-nil match.
S0.quote: Every time we get more efficient, the milk price drops by the same amount, and the processor's shareholders pocket the difference.
S0.fieldNote: Aaron is a heavy, comfortable user of technology who'd be mildly let down by a plateau. His real grievance is economic: efficiency gains flow to the processor, not to farmers. He tracks his staff's attitudes closely and sees Jodie as like-minded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is great for farming if we're smart about it. I'd be posting about it, honestly, showing people the robots and what they do. But I'd also be saying the gains need to stay with farmers and farm workers, not go up the chain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd do well out of it. I'm already halfway there. The question I'd be asking is what happens to Pete, who doesn't want to learn any of it, and to the smaller farms around me who can't afford it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a robot feed pusher and look at a weeding robot for the maize in the first year, about 60,000 all in, which our savings and a loan can cover. I'd train Jodie to run the systems and give her a raise. I'd keep Pete on the stock work he's good at, and I'd offer to show neighbours how it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited. A bit worried for Pete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd keep Pete on. Is that a business decision or a personal one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, honestly. He knows every gate and every soft patch of ground on this farm. A robot can push feed, but it can't tell you that the bottom field floods every third winter. Not yet, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a neighbour who can't afford it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say come and use mine, or let's form a group and buy one between us. I'd want a public grant for small farms, the same as we got for the slurry store.

S1.say: I'd say this is great for farming if we're smart, and I'd post about the robots I'm using. I'd also say the gains need to stay with farmers and farm workers rather than going up the chain.
S1.think: Privately I think I'd do well, since I'm already halfway there. My worry is for Pete, who doesn't want to learn it, and for smaller farms that can't afford it.
S1.do: Buys a robot feed pusher and looks at a weeding robot for the maize in the first year, about 60,000 from savings and a loan. Trains Jodie to run the systems with a raise, keeps Pete on stock work, and offers to show neighbours how it all works.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, with some worry for Pete.
S1.quote: A robot can push feed, but it can't tell you that the bottom field floods every third winter.
S1.fieldNote: Aaron is enthusiastic but keeps checking who might be left behind, which fits his progressive views. He shows real respect for Pete's local knowledge and makes it the reason to keep him. He'd also support a public grant for small farms rather than just going it alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be saying we need a plan now, not in a year. A big public fund, a basic income, rules on who owns the robots. I'd say it online and at the dairy co-op, and I'd be more political than I've ever been.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, Brookfield would probably survive, maybe even thrive, because I already know how to run a robot farm. But Jodie and Pete would be out of work, and so would half the people in town who repair tractors or drive the milk lorry. I'd be one of the winners in a town full of losers, and I don't like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate the rest of the farm as fast as I could, because if I don't, a bigger operator will buy me out. I'd keep a big cash buffer in case the milk price collapses. And I'd go to every meeting going to push for a basic income, starting with our representative's surgery next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for my own job, for the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd automate fast. What happens to Jodie and Pete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep them as long as I could, on full pay, even if the robots do the work. Pete's got four years to his pension. I'd rather pay Pete to lean on a gate than tell him after twenty years that a box on wheels has his job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ella and Finn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it's going to be strange, but we'll be all right. Ella's thirteen, she'd want to argue about whether it's fair, and she'd be right to. Finn would just want a go on the robot.

S2.say: I'd say we need a plan now, with a big public fund, a basic income and rules on who owns the robots. I'd say it online and at the dairy co-op, more politically than ever before.
S2.think: Privately I think the farm would survive and maybe thrive because I already run robots, but my staff and half the town would lose work. I'd be one of the winners in a town full of losers, and I don't like that.
S2.do: Automates the rest of the farm quickly so a bigger operator can't buy him out, and keeps a large cash buffer against a milk price collapse. Keeps Jodie and Pete on full pay as long as he can, and starts lobbying for a basic income at the representative's surgery next month.
S2.feel: Anxious, not about his own job but about his town.
S2.quote: I'd rather pay Pete to lean on a gate than tell him after twenty years that a box on wheels has his job.
S2.fieldNote: Aaron's anxiety is moral rather than personal: he expects to win while people around him lose. He'd automate quickly for defensive reasons but pay his staff to stay anyway. The fast timeline pushes him into politics more than any other scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this fairly, if we start straight away. I'd want the government to set up retraining and some kind of shared ownership of the robots for workers. I'd be talking about it at farm shows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is comfortable for me. I'd have the whole farm automated in two or three years. The extra time is for Jodie and Pete, and for the town to find its feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd pay for Jodie to do a farm robotics qualification, so she's a technician, not a farmhand. I'd help Pete plan to retire on time. I'd invest in a third milking robot and an autonomous tractor, and I'd join the regional group that's pushing for a worker-owned robot co-op.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, in the background. Mostly I'd be busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a worker-owned robot co-op realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. Nobody's done it at scale. If the robots are going to own the work, I'd like the people who used to do it to own a share of the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ella would be eighteen when it hit. I'd want her to have options, not just one path. Noor's a vet, and I'd guess vets last longer than most, so we're lucky that way.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to do this fairly if we start now. I'd talk at farm shows about government retraining and shared worker ownership of the robots.
S3.think: Privately five years is comfortable for me, as I'd automate the whole farm in two or three. The extra time is really for Jodie, Pete and the town.
S3.do: Pays for Jodie's farm robotics qualification in the first year and helps Pete plan to retire on schedule. Invests in a third milking robot and an autonomous tractor, and joins a regional group pushing for a worker-owned robot co-op.
S3.feel: Uneasy in the background but mostly busy.
S3.quote: If the robots are going to own the work, I'd like the people who used to do it to own a share of the robots.
S3.fieldNote: Aaron uses the extra time to look after his staff rather than himself. His worker-owned robot co-op idea is the most distinctive thing he says, and he admits he doesn't know if it would work. He sees his wife's job as a vet as extra protection for the household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's not waste it. I'd want schools and colleges changing now, and I'd be pushing hard for the gains to be shared through tax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine. I'd be 53, with a robot farm I've built myself and a wife with a solid job. I'd want to spend the time making sure the town comes through it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate step by step over the decade, a new piece of kit every couple of years. I'd train Jodie into a manager role. I'd also start a demo day at Brookfield every spring so other farmers can see what works and what doesn't. And I'd talk to Ella about what she wants to study, without steering her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like something I can actually shape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The processors. If they end up owning the robot farms, we're all just tenants. Ten years is long enough for the big buyers to swallow us too, if farmers don't get organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Finn, who'd be nineteen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to find something he loves that's hard to put in a box. And to learn the robots anyway, because they'll be everywhere.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift and we shouldn't waste it. I'd push for schools and colleges to change now and for the gains to be shared through tax.
S4.think: Privately I'd be fine, at 53 with a robot farm I built and a wife with a solid job. I'd want to use the time to make sure the town comes through too.
S4.do: Automates step by step over the decade, adding a piece of kit every couple of years, and trains Jodie into a manager role. Starts a yearly spring demo day at Brookfield for other farmers and talks with Ella about her studies without steering her.
S4.feel: Calm, because it feels like something he can shape.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for the big buyers to swallow us too, if farmers don't get organised.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Aaron is calm and focused on sharing what he knows with other farmers. His one lasting fear is the processors ending up owning the robot farms. He's careful to say he wouldn't steer his daughter's choice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not for me, for the town. What would help is a basic income and a public fund that lets workers and small farms own a share of the robots, set up before the robots arrive, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether the cows would be better off. I think in some ways they would, they get milked when they want. But somebody needs to watch the robots watching the cows.

headlineQuote: People think robots made me less of a farmer, but I've never known my cows better than since a machine started milking them.
portrait: Aaron Schmidt is 43 and runs Brookfield, a 180-cow dairy with maize and grass, where two robots already do the milking and he plans his day with an AI assistant. He expects to come through every scenario well, and his worry is for his two staff, Jodie and Pete, and for his town. His progressive views show in his ideas: basic income, public grants for small farms and a worker-owned robot co-op. He's calm in the slower scenarios, anxious in the two-year one because others would lose while he wins, and keeps returning to the processors who take farmers' gains.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, not for himself but for his staff and the town, who'd lose work fast.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income and a public fund letting workers and small farms own a share of the robots, set up before the robots arrive.
